taxonomy.note: Accepted by current Kew/POWO. Three accepted varieties are recognized globally; learner stays species-level.

evidence: BONAP/NAPA maps Phyla nodiflora at county level and treats it as native in Texas.
Hays County — UT Plant Resources Center's Purola Preserve flora lists P. nodiflora among plants occurring naturally and not introduced.
Travis County — UT Plant Resources Center's Travis County Verbenaceae herbarium index includes P. nodiflora; additional wild Travis records are documented at Emma Long and Reimers Ranch.
Williamson County — UT Plant Resources Center provides a detailed county treatment for P. nodiflora.
target_zone_range.guardrail: Frogfruit is widely planted as a groundcover. County proof uses native-flora/herbarium treatments, not landscape plantings.

morphology.look_here_first: Look at the leaf before the flower head. Frogfruit has opposite oblanceolate-to-elliptic leaves that are usually widest beyond the middle, with the teeth concentrated on the upper/distal half. Then confirm the creeping stems rooting at nodes and the dense cylindrical flower spike on a long axillary peduncle.
diagnostic_traits: perennial clonal groundcover with prostrate to procumbent stems
creeping stems root at buried or contacting nodes
leaf blades oblanceolate to elliptic, commonly widest beyond the middle
leaf margins serrate mainly above the midpoint, often fewer than six teeth per side
single dense spherical-to-cylindrical flower spikes arise on axillary peduncles
tiny white to pink/purplish flowers open around the spike, often with yellow/orange/purple throats

confusers.separator: The best leaf split: P. nodiflora is usually widest beyond the middle and its teeth are concentrated in the distal half; P. lanceolata is widest nearer the middle and the teeth extend farther down the blade.
Wedgeleaf frogfruit has a more distinctly wedge-shaped leaf architecture. Use several mature leaves rather than one odd leaf, because Phyla leaf shape varies along a shoot.

Glandularia can also form low mats with verbena-like flowers, but its flowers are much larger and borne in more open terminal heads/spikes; Phyla has tiny flowers packed into a compact button/cylinder on a naked axillary peduncle.

diagnostic_roles: whole creeping mat and rooting nodes
single mature leaf showing widest point and tooth position
opposite leaf pair at a node
side view of compact cylindrical flower spike
photo_verification.provenance_note: The highest-value training image is a mature leaf laid flat enough to see where the blade is widest and where serrations begin.
